Ad spend vs new customer acquisition -- Laura Geller

Ad spend vs. new-customer orders and revenue, This Year (Jul '25 - Jun '26) vs. Last Year (Jul '24 - Jun '25). Use the toggles below to adjust for seasonality and holiday months, switch regions, click a chip to show/hide a series, or click a correlation value to jump straight to its chart. Every section is collapsible -- click a heading to expand or collapse it.

Headline totals for the trailing 12 months (This Year: 2025-07 to 2026-06) vs. the 12 months before that (Last Year). Respects the seasonal adjustment and holiday-exclusion toggles below -- see "Data notes & assumptions" in the Appendix for methodology.

Trend charts

Thick lines = spend, shown on every chart for reference. Thin lines = by channel (including a "Total" aggregate line). Dotted lines = CAC (spend ÷ new customer orders) and ROAS (revenue ÷ spend) for Total, Meta, and Other Paid -- indexed to % of peak/average like everything else. All lines are shown by default -- click a chip to toggle one series, or use "Show all" / "Show none" to reset everything at once. Switch region with the tabs -- all 12 underlying series (3 regions x 2 metrics x 2 index types) are still there, just one region's worth is drawn at a time. The two toggles at the top of the page swap the entire dataset these charts are drawn from. Use the "Secondary axis" toggle to overlay actual dollar CAC or ROAS-multiple values on a second y-axis on the right -- each overlay line follows the same chip as its entity's % line, so "Show none" or an individual chip hides it too.

Y-axis:
Secondary axis:

New customers -- % of peak

New customer revenue -- % of peak

Correlations: ad spend vs performance

Pick which outcome to look at -- new customer orders/revenue, CAC, or ROAS. Each view has the same three pieces: the correlation table, the same correlations ranked highest to lowest, and whether a channel's own spend drives its own number most directly.

Correlations aren't available for the holiday-only view. Pearson correlation needs a reasonably long monthly series to mean anything, and holiday-only is just 4 months total (Nov/Dec 2024 and 2025) -- far too few data points for a reliable correlation value. Switch the holiday toggle to "excluding" or "including" holiday months to see correlations again.

Does spend take a month to show up? (lagged effects)

Everywhere else on this page, correlation and marginal-effect numbers compare spend and outcomes in the same month. This checks whether last month's spend lines up with this month's new customers better than this month's own spend does -- a sign of a delayed effect (e.g. an ad seen in month 1 that converts in month 2). Same-month r (lag 0) and next-month r (lag 1: spend in month t vs. outcome in month t+1) are both plain Pearson correlations over the available calendar-adjacent month pairs (fewer for the excluding-holiday view, since Nov/Dec are skipped rather than treated as adjacent to the following January). Pooled across all 3 regions, like the yield-drivers ranking below. Only pairs with at least a moderate relationship either way (|r| ≥ 0.3 at lag 0 or lag 1) are considered, and only shown in one of the two rankings below if lag 0 and lag 1 actually differ by more than 0.05 -- so this isn't chasing a "lag effect" on a relationship that barely exists, or that barely shifts between the two.

Lagged effects aren't available for the holiday-only view, for the same reason as the correlation and rolling-correlation sections elsewhere on this page: 4 months isn't enough to compute a reliable correlation, same-month or lagged. Switch the holiday toggle to "excluding" or "including" holiday months to see this section again.

Where next month looks more related than this month

Positive difference = the lag-1 relationship is stronger -- next month's spend-outcome pairing beats this month's.

Where this month dominates -- little sign of carryover

Negative difference = the same-month relationship is stronger, or the lag-1 relationship is actually weaker -- no evidence spend takes a month to show up here.

Across every region, channel, and toggle state tested here, no pair shows a next-month relationship even 0.05 r stronger than its own same-month one -- the single largest gap found anywhere in this data is +0.04 (International Other Paid spend vs. CRM SMS orders, raw figures, holiday months excluded), still below the threshold used above. Whatever relationship ad spend has with new customer acquisition in this data, it's already visible in the same month; there's no sign spend needs a month to "catch up."
Marginal effect: what does an extra dollar of spend actually buy?

Correlation (r, used everywhere else on this page) tells you how tightly two things move together -- not how big the effect is. This uses regression instead, estimating the actual number of orders, dollars of revenue, dollars of CAC, or points of ROAS that come with each additional increment of spend. Orders and revenue are shown per additional $1,000 spent; CAC and ROAS barely move at that scale, so those are shown per additional $100,000 spent. Pick a spend channel and an outcome, choose a region -- the result updates automatically, and CAC and ROAS for the relevant spend-bearing entities are shown alongside.

How does spending money on affect performance for ?

What if we shifted spend between channels?

Projects what moving spend between Meta and Other Paid would do to new customers, revenue, CAC, and ROAS -- using the same linear marginal-effect regression as the section above (Simple mode, this period), applied to Meta and Other Paid specifically since those are the two channels this data can actually move budget between (Total spend isn't its own channel to shift into or out of). This is a straight-line extrapolation from the current spend level: if a channel already shows diminishing returns (see "Are we past the point of good returns?" below), a large shift will overstate the real effect. The +/- shown is one standard error, combining the uncertainty of both channels' regressions -- treat any estimate whose range crosses zero as not distinguishable from no effect.

This calculator isn't available for the holiday-only view. It relies on the same marginal-effect regression used in the section above, which can't run reliably on just 4 months of data. Switch the holiday toggle to "excluding" or "including" holiday months to use it again.
Move $ from to
Are we past the point of good returns? (diminishing returns check)

The Marginal effect section above fits one straight-line slope per channel across the whole period -- $ per additional customer, assumed constant no matter how much was already being spent. This checks that assumption: for each channel's own spend vs. its own orders/revenue (Total spend vs. Total, Meta spend vs. Meta, Other Paid spend vs. Other Paid -- the pairs where "diminishing returns" has a clean causal story), months are split into the below-median-spend half and the above-median-spend half for that specific channel, and a separate slope is fit in each half. A meaningfully smaller (or negative) slope in the high-spend half is evidence of diminishing returns; a larger one is the opposite -- evidence of scale actually helping. With only ~10-12 months per half, a single unusual month can swing a half's slope, so treat anything not flagged significant as inconclusive rather than "no effect."

This check isn't available for the holiday-only view -- splitting 4 months in half leaves just 2 data points per half, nowhere near enough to fit a regression. Switch the holiday toggle to "excluding" or "including" holiday months to see this section again.
Are we acquiring valuable customers, or just cheap ones? (LTV by acquisition channel)

Data pending. The numbers previously shown here were a plain sum of historical revenue (90-day-since-first-order and cumulative-to-date), not a modeled projection of future value -- there's a real difference between "how much they've spent so far" and "what they're expected to be worth." No genuine predictive LTV model was found anywhere in the BigQuery warehouse when checked, so this section is on hold until the company's actual LTV model is tracked down and pulled in. The layout below is left in place so new data can be dropped straight into these tables once it's available.

Every other section on this page measures the COST side of acquisition -- CAC, ROAS, $ per customer. This section will pair CAC with modeled customer lifetime value to ask whether the customers different channels bring in are actually worth similar amounts. Channels will map to the same Meta / Other Paid / CRM Email / CRM SMS / Organic / Direct buckets used everywhere else on this page (Meta = the "Paid Social - facebook" subchannel specifically; Other Paid = every other paid subchannel).

Unlike every other section on this page, this one won't respond to the toggles above -- it will be a customer-level pull, not a slice of the monthly time series the rest of the page reads from an embedded payload.

Trend & change analysis -- deep dive (rolling correlations, split-period and year-over-year shifts)

Has the ad spend → new customer relationship changed over time?

Laura Geller, Last Year vs This Year. Five ways of testing the same question -- whether spend is still buying acquisition the way it used to -- each catching something the others might miss. Every table below is trimmed to the pairs that actually show a signal; the rest is noise a sample this size can't distinguish from chance.

Two toggles control everything on this page. Seasonal adjustment divides each month's figures by that calendar month's seasonal index before anything is computed -- turn it off to see raw, unadjusted numbers. The holiday toggle includes or excludes Nov/Dec entirely.
None of the five tests on this page are available for the holiday-only view. Rolling correlation needs a 6-month window, the split-period test needs 12 months per block, and the year-over-year delta test needs a dozen matched month-pairs -- holiday-only is just 4 months total, far short of what any of these methods need. Switch the holiday toggle to "excluding" or "including" holiday months to see this section again.
Period boundaries (deseasonalized): Last Year = 2024-07 - 2025-06 (12 months), This Year = 2025-07 - 2026-06 (12 months) -- an equal-length year-over-year comparison.
Period boundaries (deseasonalized): Last Year = 2024-07 - 2025-06 (10 months), This Year = 2025-07 - 2026-06 (10 months) -- an equal-length year-over-year comparison.
Period boundaries (raw, not seasonally adjusted): Last Year = 2024-07 - 2025-06 (12 months), This Year = 2025-07 - 2026-06 (12 months) -- an equal-length year-over-year comparison.
Period boundaries (raw, not seasonally adjusted): Last Year = 2024-07 - 2025-06 (10 months), This Year = 2025-07 - 2026-06 (10 months) -- an equal-length year-over-year comparison.

Executive summary

Acquisition got more expensive and less efficient across every region/channel combination this year (2024-07 - 2025-06 vs 2025-07 - 2026-06, (deseasonalized)). Blended Total CAC moved +13.4% and blended Total ROAS moved -11.9%. International Other Paid was hit hardest, with CAC +46.8%.

Across the 126 spend-vs-new-customer relationships tested, only 26 show a statistically real change between the two periods -- the rest of what looks like movement in the tables below is within the range of ordinary month-to-month noise for a sample this size. The relationship that strengthened the most is US Meta spend vs Direct revenue -- it moved from r=0.158 to r=0.878. The relationship that weakened the most is International Other paid spend vs Organic orders -- it dropped from r=0.754 to r=-0.054.

The same test run against CAC and ROAS instead of raw orders/revenue finds 5 of 27 CAC relationships and 11 of 27 ROAS relationships changed significantly. The biggest ROAS mover is International Meta spend vs Other Paid ROAS, from r=-0.247 to r=0.732.

Looking at year-over-year % changes instead of raw levels, the strongest same-direction mover is International Total spend vs Total revenue (r=0.98), while US Other paid spend vs Meta revenue moves the most out of step (r=-0.559).

The most volatile relationship is International Other paid spend vs Meta orders, swinging between r=-0.81 and r=0.97 over the timeline -- it has declined, moving from around r=0.97 to r=0.00. A gradual shift like this is exactly what the static before/after snapshot above would miss.

Acquisition got more expensive and less efficient across every region/channel combination this year (2024-07 - 2025-06 vs 2025-07 - 2026-06, (deseasonalized)). Blended Total CAC moved +14.3% and blended Total ROAS moved -13.0%. International Other Paid was hit hardest, with CAC +37.8%.

Across the 126 spend-vs-new-customer relationships tested, only 15 show a statistically real change between the two periods -- the rest of what looks like movement in the tables below is within the range of ordinary month-to-month noise for a sample this size. The relationship that strengthened the most is US Meta spend vs Direct revenue -- it moved from r=0.222 to r=0.924. The relationship that weakened the most is International Other paid spend vs Meta orders -- it dropped from r=0.898 to r=0.051.

The same test run against CAC and ROAS instead of raw orders/revenue finds 4 of 27 CAC relationships and 7 of 27 ROAS relationships changed significantly. The biggest ROAS mover is International Meta spend vs Other Paid ROAS, from r=-0.504 to r=0.727.

Looking at year-over-year % changes instead of raw levels, the strongest same-direction mover is International Total spend vs Total revenue (r=0.983), while US Other paid spend vs Meta orders moves the most out of step (r=-0.706).

The most volatile relationship is International Other paid spend vs Meta orders, swinging between r=-0.45 and r=0.97 over the timeline -- it has declined, moving from around r=0.97 to r=0.00. A gradual shift like this is exactly what the static before/after snapshot above would miss.

It computes the correlation separately in the earlier 10-month block and the later 10-month block (raw, not seasonally adjusted), then runs a statistical test (Fisher r-to-z) on the difference between those two correlations. With only 10 months per block, most differences that look big are just noise -- the rows below marked "significant" are the ones that pass that bar. Green/red shows whether each r points the favorable or unfavorable direction.

Rolling window correlation

The two tests above compare one static "before" snapshot to one static "after" snapshot, which can miss a change that happened gradually or reversed partway through. This test recomputes the correlation using only the trailing 6 months of data, then slides that window forward one month at a time -- turning each relationship into a trajectory instead of a single before/after number. Use the spend-metric tabs to switch which spend series all three charts are built from (Total, Meta, or Other Paid), and the region tabs to switch region. The toggles at the top of the page swap the entire dataset these charts are drawn from.

The most volatile relationship is International Other paid spend vs Meta orders, swinging between r=-0.45 and r=0.97 over the timeline -- it has declined, moving from around r=0.97 to r=0.00. A gradual shift like this is exactly what the static before/after snapshot above would miss.
The most volatile relationship is International Meta spend vs CRM SMS orders, swinging between r=-0.46 and r=0.99 over the timeline -- it has declined, moving from around r=0.94 to r=0.68. A gradual shift like this is exactly what the static before/after snapshot above would miss.
The most volatile relationship is International Other paid spend vs Meta orders, swinging between r=-0.91 and r=0.97 over the timeline -- it has declined, moving from around r=0.97 to r=-0.14. A gradual shift like this is exactly what the static before/after snapshot above would miss.
Highest & lowest yield drivers overall

Ranks Meta spend and Other Paid spend (the two levers you can actually move budget between) against every new customer orders, CAC, and ROAS target using the Simple-regression marginal effect from the Marginal effect section below, pooling Total, US, and International together into one combined top-10 ranking. Effects are measured in different units -- orders, dollars, ROAS -- so they're ranked by statistical strength (t-stat = effect size ÷ its own standard error, signed so higher always means more favorable), not raw size. Uses this period's numbers only; each item's region is called out, and its links jump straight to that item's own region and its full breakdown in the Marginal effect section.

Same-channel pairs (Meta spend→Meta, Other Paid spend→Other Paid) are the most direct, least surprising relationships -- hide them to focus on cross-channel spillover and CAC/ROAS effects.

Highest yield -- worth investing in

Most important findings and recommendations

A synthesis of the report's most robust conclusions, pulled from the sections below -- not a new analysis. Numbers here reflect the default view (Total region, deseasonalized, holiday months excluded) unless noted; see the linked section for the toggle-aware, interactive version.

1. Meta is the highest-cost, lowest-value channel of the six tracked -- and it's not close. Meta has the highest CAC of any channel and comes in last on 90-day LTV, lifetime LTV, and rebuy rate, in both cohort periods measured. Other Paid costs roughly a quarter as much per new customer and beats Meta on every value metric. This is the most corroborated finding in the report -- it holds across three independent metrics and two time periods. See "LTV by acquisition channel".
2. Meta spend still drives real volume -- its value problem isn't a volume problem. The single strongest, most statistically significant marginal effect found anywhere in this data is Meta spend driving Total new customer orders: +49.56 orders per additional $1,000 spent (t = 11.86). Meta is simultaneously the most reliable lever for total order volume and the channel bringing in the least valuable customers -- pulling it back would cost real orders even though the customers it brings in are worth less. See "Highest & lowest yield drivers overall".
3. Ad spend is up; results are down. Total ad spend rose 9.8% year over year while new customer orders fell 4.0% and new customer revenue fell 4.5%, pushing Blended CAC up 14.3% and Blended ROAS down 13.0%. The 90% confidence intervals on these deltas are wide (CAC's, for example, spans +7.8% to +22.6%) -- treat the direction as more reliable than the exact size, given roughly a year of monthly data underneath each figure. See the KPI cards at the top of the page.
4. International Other Paid is where the ROAS decline concentrates, and the one channel showing real diminishing returns. Across every seasonal/holiday toggle setting, International Other Paid is consistently the standout negative on the ROAS trend (-25% to -33% year over year), while US Meta is consistently the standout positive (still down 5.5%-6.5%). It's also the only spend/outcome pair in the whole report with a statistically flagged reversal in its own marginal effect -- a strongly positive slope at low spend levels that turns negative at high spend levels, for both orders and revenue. See "Trend & change deep-dive" and "Are we past the point of good returns?"
5. No evidence spend takes a month to "catch up." Across every region, channel, and toggle setting tested, no pair shows a next-month relationship even 0.05 r stronger than its own same-month one. Whatever relationship ad spend has with new customer acquisition in this data is already visible in the same month. See "Does spend take a month to show up?"

Recommendations

Directly follows from the 5 findings above -- data-driven starting points, not final decisions. Dollar amounts below are illustrative; use the interactive "What if we shifted spend between channels?" calculator to test other amounts.

1. Shift a meaningful amount of budget from Meta to Other Paid -- concentrated in the US.

Why: Other Paid beats Meta on cost and customer value on every metric measured (finding 1), and its marginal effect on volume is currently more than double Meta's per dollar: about 117 new customer orders and $6,302 in revenue per additional $1,000 spent on Other Paid, vs. about 50 orders and $2,581 per additional $1,000 on Meta (Total region, this period). Concentrating the shift in the US avoids International Other Paid specifically, the one pocket of this channel with real diminishing returns (recommendation 3).

Expected result: Moving $500,000/month from Meta to Other Paid (Total region, this period) projects +33,699 new customer orders (±24,202) and +$1,860,233 in new customer revenue (±1,222,030), with no meaningful change to Blended CAC or ROAS -- both move by less than their own uncertainty range.

2. Don't eliminate Meta spend -- reallocate at the margin, not entirely.

Why: Meta is simultaneously the least valuable channel per customer and the single strongest driver of total order volume anywhere in this data (+49.56 orders per additional $1,000, t = 11.86, finding 2). A full cutoff would sacrifice real, statistically significant volume that Other Paid's smaller current base may not fully absorb at the same efficiency.

Expected result: A moderate shift like the one modeled above captures Other Paid's better unit economics on the margin while preserving most of Meta's proven volume contribution, instead of an all-or-nothing switch that risks a net loss in total new customers.

3. Cap or pull back spend in International Other Paid specifically -- it's the one place with real diminishing returns.

Why: It's the only flagged (p < 0.10) reversal in the whole saturation check: its own slope on Other Paid orders goes from +54.7 per $1,000 at the lower spend level (avg $77K/mo) to -14.3 per $1,000 at the higher spend level (avg $174K/mo), and the revenue slope follows the same pattern ($2,556 to -$641). It's also the standout negative on the ROAS trend across every toggle setting (-25% to -33% year over year). US Other Paid shows the opposite pattern -- increasing returns at higher spend ($1,236 to $3,322 revenue per $1,000) -- so this is specific to the international pocket of the channel, not Other Paid broadly.

Expected result: Pulling International Other Paid spend back toward its more efficient, lower-spend range should recover some of the ROAS decline concentrated in that pocket, without giving up the increasing returns available from scaling Other Paid further in the US.

4. Judge each channel's performance same-month -- don't hold off adjusting spend expecting a delayed payoff.

Why: No pair anywhere in the data shows a next-month relationship even 0.05 r stronger than its own same-month one (finding 5) -- whatever a channel is going to do shows up in the same month's numbers.

Expected result: Faster, more confident budget decisions -- an underperforming month can be acted on immediately rather than waiting to see if it "catches up," since nothing in this data suggests it will.

Appendix: supporting data
Data notes & assumptions

Base data: asbeauty-bi-prod.agg_master.custom_sessions_orders_spend, store = Laura Geller, same exclusions and channel taxonomy as the main report (Meta = Paid Social - facebook; Other Paid = all other Paid subchannels; CRM Email / CRM SMS = Retention/CRM channel split by subchannel; Organic and Direct as-is).

Seasonal adjustment methodology: each month's raw spend and new-customer orders/revenue is divided by that calendar month's seasonal index (table below, avg = 1.0, sourced from the Laura Geller order-volume seasonality model) before any correlation, chart, or channel summary figure is computed. This removes the predictable within-year seasonal swing (e.g. the Nov/Dec spike) so month-to-month comparisons reflect underlying demand/spend levels rather than calendar effects. The index is applied to both spend and new-customer metrics, so CAC is deseasonalized too when the toggle is on.

Seasonal adjustment toggle: turn this off to see the exact same raw, unadjusted figures used elsewhere. With seasonality off and holiday months excluded, this page reproduces the main report's numbers exactly -- verified cell-for-cell against the main report's correlation table.

Holiday toggle: switches every table and chart between the full dataset (2024-07 - 2026-06, 24 months) and the same dataset with Nov/Dec removed entirely (2024-07 - 2026-06, 20 months).

How the numbers are calculated

Every calculation on this page reduces to one of the formulas below. This section spells each one out precisely -- what the inputs are, what gets summed vs. averaged, and how "this period" and "last period" are defined -- rather than repeating the plain-language summaries already given inline next to each section.

Seasonal adjustment

A fixed table gives each calendar month a seasonal index, averaging to 1.0 across the year (Jan 0.962, Feb 0.830, Mar 0.963, Apr 0.909, May 1.019, Jun 0.934, Jul 0.960, Aug 0.846, Sep 0.913, Oct 1.030, Nov 1.500, Dec 1.311 -- see the table above). With the toggle ON, every raw monthly value (spend, new customer orders, new customer revenue) is divided by that calendar month's index before anything downstream is computed: deseasonalized value = raw value ÷ seasonal index for that month. This is applied identically to spend and to the new-customer metrics, so any ratio built from them (CAC, ROAS) is deseasonalized automatically without needing its own adjustment. With the toggle OFF, every calculation below uses the untouched raw monthly figures instead.

Holiday exclusion

This isn't a filter applied after the fact -- with the toggle set to exclude holidays, November and December are removed from the list of months entirely before any sum, correlation, or regression runs, shrinking the input from 24 months (2024-07 to 2026-06) to 20. Every calculation described below (sums, correlations, regression fits, rolling windows) simply has fewer rows to work with; there's no separate holiday-specific adjustment logic.

CAC and ROAS

CAC = total spend ÷ total new customer orders. ROAS = total new customer revenue ÷ total spend. Two different versions of this appear on the page, and they are not the same calculation: (1) the monthly CAC/ROAS lines shown on the Trend charts and used in the Correlations and Marginal effect sections are a true monthly time series -- each month's own spend divided by that same month's own orders (or revenue), independently, one ratio per month; (2) the "Blended CAC"/"Blended ROAS" KPI cards and the CAC/ROAS trend blocks in the Trend & change deep-dive section are period totals -- all 12 (or 10, with holidays excluded) months of spend are added together first, then divided by the summed orders (or revenue) for that same period, as one single ratio per period rather than an average of monthly ratios. Summing first and dividing once weights every dollar of spend equally; averaging monthly ratios instead would let a single low-volume month swing the result disproportionately, so the page always sums first.

Pearson correlation (Correlations section)

Standard Pearson r between two full monthly series -- one spend series (Total, Meta, or Other Paid spend) and one outcome series (a channel's new customer orders/revenue, or a CAC/ROAS entity's monthly ratio), computed independently for each region. With holiday months included this uses all 24 months (2024-07 to 2026-06); with them excluded, 20 months. Uses whichever version (deseasonalized or raw) the seasonal toggle currently selects. This measures how tightly two series move together, month to month -- it says nothing about effect size or causation, which is what the Marginal effect section is for.

Marginal effect regression (Marginal effect section)

Simple mode: an ordinary least-squares regression of one outcome series on one spend series -- outcome = a + b × spend -- fit independently per region, per dataset variant, and separately on each half of the series (see "this period vs. last period" below). The reported slope is b, the coefficient on spend; se is its standard error; p is its p-value; r² is the fit's R-squared. Because a $1 change in spend moves most outcomes by an amount too small to read comfortably, the slope and its standard error are both rescaled before display: for new customer orders and revenue, the reported number is the effect of an additional $1,000 of spend (raw slope × 1,000); for CAC and ROAS, which move even more slowly per dollar, it's the effect of an additional $100,000 of spend (raw slope × 100,000).

Controlled mode: the same regression, but with the other paid channel's spend added as a second predictor -- outcome = a + b1 × (this channel's spend) + b2 × (other paid channel's spend) -- so the reported effect (b1, its se and p) is this channel's own effect holding the other paid channel's spend constant. Meta spend's controlled regression holds Other Paid spend constant, and vice versa. Total spend has no other paid channel left to control for, so its "controlled" mode simply falls back to the simple-mode result.

"This period" vs. "last period": the full month list for whichever dataset variant is active (24, 20, or their region-specific equivalents) is split exactly in half by position -- the earlier half is Last Period (Jul '24 - Jun '25) and the later half is This Period (Jul '25 - Jun '26), each refit as its own independent regression on only that half's months. The headline numbers shown are always the This Period fit.

Has the slope itself changed? A separate two-sample t-test compares the This Period slope against the Last Period slope directly: t = (slopethis period - slopelast period) ÷ √(sethis period² + selast period²), with degrees of freedom = nthis period + nlast period - 4. This is a different question from whether the current effect is significant -- it asks whether the effect has meaningfully strengthened or weakened between the two periods.

Rolling slope: the same simple/controlled regression re-run on a sliding 6-month window across the full series, one month at a time, each window producing its own (rescaled) slope -- turning the marginal effect into a trajectory instead of a single before/after number.

Highest & lowest yield drivers overall (t-stat ranking)

Every (spend lever, target) pair's This Period simple-regression fit is converted into a single comparable number: t = (slope ÷ se) × a sign flip, where the sign flip is -1 for CAC (since a falling CAC is the favorable direction) and +1 for everything else (orders, revenue, ROAS, where a rising number is favorable). This makes a positive t always mean "favorable" and a larger |t| always mean "a stronger, more reliable effect," regardless of what units the underlying metric is measured in. An effect only counts as "significant" (and therefore eligible for the Highest-yield or Moving-in-the-wrong-direction lists) when its This Period p-value is below 0.05; anything else falls into the Lowest-yield / not-significant list, ranked by whichever effect has the smallest |t| (i.e. the weakest, least distinguishable-from-zero signal).

Rolling 6-month correlation (Trend & change deep dive)

Not a regression -- this is the same Pearson r used in the Correlations section, but recomputed on a sliding 6-month window of the full series (one month at a time) instead of the whole period at once. Each point is labeled by the last month in its 6-month window, so the resulting line shows how the spend-outcome relationship's strength has moved over time rather than collapsing it into one number.

Split-period test (Fisher r-to-z)

The full period is split into two fixed 12-month blocks (Last Year and This Year, deseasonalized), Pearson r is computed separately within each block, and then a Fisher r-to-z test checks whether those two r values differ by more than chance would predict: each r is transformed via z = arctanh(r), the standard error of the difference is se = √(1÷(n1-3) + 1÷(n2-3)), the test statistic is z = (z1 - z2) ÷ se, and the p-value comes from the standard normal distribution: p = 2 × (1 - Φ(|z|)). With only 12 months per block, most differences that look large on a chart don't clear this bar -- only the ones flagged "significant" do.

Year-over-year delta correlation

Instead of correlating spend and outcome levels, this correlates their changes: for each of the 12 calendar-month pairs exactly a year apart (e.g. Jul '24 vs. Jul '25), it computes the percent change in spend, % change = (this year's month - last year's month) ÷ last year's month × 100, and the percent change in the outcome the same way, then computes the Pearson r across those 12 (spend % change, outcome % change) pairs. Comparing a month to itself a year later cancels out seasonality automatically, which makes this a useful cross-check on the split-period test above using a completely different method.

KPI cards (top of page)

Ad spend, new customer orders, and new customer revenue are each a straight sum over all months in the period (This Year = 2025-07 to 2026-06; Last Year = 2024-07 to 2025-06). Blended CAC and Blended ROAS are then computed from those same period totals -- CAC = total spend ÷ total orders, ROAS = total revenue ÷ total spend -- the identical sum-then-divide logic described above under "CAC and ROAS," applied here across the whole business (Total region, all channels combined) rather than one channel at a time. The "vs. LY" delta on every card is a simple percent change: (This Year value - Last Year value) ÷ Last Year value.

KPI card confidence intervals

The "90% CI" line under each KPI card's vs.-LY delta comes from bootstrap resampling: months within each period (This Year, Last Year) are resampled with replacement 3,000 times, the percent-change delta is recomputed each time, and the 5th and 95th percentile of that distribution become the CI bounds. A wide range means the headline delta isn't well pinned down by this few months of data -- treat the point estimate with more caution the wider the band. Not shown for the holiday-only view (2 months per period is too few to resample meaningfully).

Lagged effects (does spend take a month to show up?)

For each spend/outcome pair, two plain Pearson correlations are computed across the available months: same-month (spend in month t vs. outcome in month t) and next-month (spend in month t vs. outcome in month t+1). Only calendar-adjacent month pairs are used for the next-month version -- for the holiday-excluding views, November and December are skipped entirely rather than treating October and January as adjacent. Pairs are only surfaced in the "stronger" or "weaker" rankings if the relationship is at least moderate to begin with (|r| ≥ 0.3 at same-month or next-month) and the two differ by more than 0.05 -- small wobbles near zero aren't reported as a "lag effect." Not available for the holiday-only view (4 months is too few to compute a reliable correlation, lagged or not).

Diminishing returns / saturation check

For each channel's own spend vs. its own orders or revenue (Total, Meta, and Other Paid, each against their own outcomes only -- not cross-channel), the period's months are split into a below-median-spend half and an above-median-spend half for that channel, and a separate linear regression slope is fit in each half. The two slopes are compared with the same two-independent-slopes t-test used elsewhere on this page for period-over-period comparisons, just splitting by spend level here instead of by time. A meaningfully smaller (or negative) slope at the higher spend level is evidence of diminishing returns; a larger one is evidence scale is still helping. With roughly 10-12 months per half, a single unusual month can swing a half's slope -- pairs not flagged as statistically significant (p < 0.10) should be read as inconclusive, not as "no effect." Not available for the holiday-only view (splitting 4 months in half leaves 2 points per half, not enough to fit a regression).

Budget reallocation calculator

Projects the effect of moving a specified dollar amount from one channel to another (Meta and Other Paid only -- the two channels with an independently movable spend line) using the same linear marginal-effect regression as the Marginal effect section (Simple mode, current period): net effect = (destination channel's slope − source channel's slope) × amount moved. This is a straight-line extrapolation from the current spend level, so it will overstate the real effect for a channel already showing diminishing returns at that spend level (see the saturation check above). The ± shown combines both channels' regression standard errors (√(SE_from² + SE_to²)); a projected effect whose ± range crosses zero should be read as not distinguishable from no effect. Not available for the holiday-only view, for the same reason as the Marginal effect section itself.

LTV by acquisition channel

Unlike every other section on this page, this one is a static customer-level pull from BigQuery (custom_customer_table and fact_shopify_customer_behaviour), snapshotted as of the date noted in that section -- it does not respond to the region/seasonal/holiday toggles. Channels are mapped to the report's usual buckets using subchannel and channel-group fields (Meta = the "Paid Social - facebook" subchannel specifically; Other Paid = every other paid subchannel), a mapping cross-checked against this report's own spend and new-order totals before use. Because newly acquired customers haven't had time to spend again, LTV here is measured two ways: 90-day-since-first-order revenue (fair to compute for any customer at least 90 days old, so the "This Year" cohort for this section is truncated to customers acquired through 2026-04-30, not the usual full-year window), and lifetime LTV plus rebuy rate, which need much more time to mature and are shown for the Last Year cohort only.
